newsitem.title: USA: U.S., California officials reach wetland agreement.
newsitem.headline: U.S., California officials reach wetland agreement.

text.p: A $90 million agreement to create one of the largest coastal wetland reserves in southern California was completed on Tuesday, federal and state officials said.
The agreement, which will restore and permanently preserve 880 acres (356 hectares) of wetlands at Bolsa Chica in Orange County, resolves a 20-year controversy over the wetlands' future.

Under the agreement the Bolsa Chica lowlands would be publicly managed as a wetland habitat for a variety of fish, migratory birds and other wildlife and aquatic species, the officials said. Restoration would begin in 1999 following an environmental review and cleanup.

"This is truly one of the last undeveloped coastal wetlands of any significant size in Southern California, an area that is under the greatest development pressure of anywhere in the nation," said George Frampton, assistant secretary of the Interior for Fish, Wildlife and Parks.
While in favor of the wetland's protection, an official with the environmental group Sierra Club blasted the Bolsa Chica deal because of its cost.
"This land could have been acquired for a fraction of the cost," attorney Mark Massara, who directs Sierra Club's coastal program said. "It's corporate welfare at its worst."

Under the agreement, the lands would be acquired by the California State Lands Commission, which must approve the purchase decision and recommendations of the resources agencies. The commission will vote on the issue on Wednesday.
California taxpayers would incur almost no costs of the purchase and no costs from restoration or cleanup of contaminants at the site, state and federal officials said.

Under the plan, the State Lands Commission would acquire the 880 acres (356 hectares) of lowlands from the Koll Real Estate Group with $78 million in funding from the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, state officials said.
The $12 million balance for purchase and restoration of the wetlands would be raised mostly from the interest that will accrue on the $78 million contribution from the ports.

In return for the funds, the state said the ports would receive environmental "mitigation credits," which will allow the ports to proceed with their expansion plans. The ports need the credits in order to satisfy a series of state and federal laws that protect the environment.

The deal will create a permanent 1,200-acre (485 hectares) wetlands reserve at Bolsa Chica near Huntington Beach. The reserve will be the third largest coastal wetland in southern California, the federal government said.
The state said cleanup and restoration would take about 25 years, although the vast majority of the work should be completed by 2001.
